overview: The atlas labels one huge color “Iranian pastoralists” from 1500 to 500 BCE. Its decoded polygon does not match modern Iran: sampled Tehran, Tabriz, Hamadan, Isfahan, Shiraz and Susa lie outside, while Yazd, Kerman, Khorasan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Kashgar lie inside. No single people called that whole shape home. Across deserts, river oases, foothills and high valleys, some families moved herds seasonally; others lived in mudbrick settlements, farmed irrigated plots, made pottery, spun fibers, worked bronze and later iron, or exchanged grain, stone and metal. Sheep, goats, cattle and horses mattered differently by place. Wheat, barley, millet, peas and gathered foods kept “pastoralists” from being a meat-only stereotype. Archaeology, radiocarbon dates, plant remains, animal bones, isotopes and ancient DNA each answer different questions. Reconstructed Iranian languages cannot be read from pots or genes, and later Avestan or Old Persian texts cannot supply everybody's voice. At 500 BCE the atlas redraws most tested points as the Achaemenid Empire, while Kashgar becomes blank. That is a map seam, not the disappearance of all local communities.

periods.title: 1500 to 1000 BCE: post-Oxus transitions and many mixed economies
periods.summary: The first atlas interval spans the final occupations of some Oxus or BMAC centers, seasonal camps on the Murghab fringe, and the emergence of Yaz I traditions in several southern Central Asian oases. Local chronologies overlap, so neither handmade pottery nor new ancestry marks one simultaneous migration.

periods.title: 1000 to 700 BCE: oasis settlements, handmade wares and early iron
periods.summary: During the second exact interval, Yaz traditions appear across several farming oases while mobile herding, mixed cropping and regional exchange continue. Mudbrick platforms, handmade painted pottery and the first uncommon iron objects vary by site; they do not define one state, language or way of life.

periods.title: 700 to 500 BCE: larger centers, stronger links and an imperial atlas seam
periods.summary: In the final interval, some centers become more fortified, wheel-made pottery increases and iron tools spread. Political names become historically clearer only near the end. The 500 BCE atlas replacement by Achaemenid and other labels compresses an uneven sixth-century transformation into one clean cartographic boundary.

sections.title: Read the atlas label with a very large pinch of salt

items.text: The exact indexed record says “Iranian pastoralists,” kind “culture,” with approximate dates from 1500 to 500 BCE. Coverage records three continuous border intervals and no earlier card, summary or researched override. Those are database facts. They do not establish one ethnicity, Iranian-speaking nation, ancestry, government or uniform herding economy.

At 1500 BCE the target is one Polygon with 186 positions and bounds from about 50 to 82 degrees east and 25 to 46 degrees north. Yazd, Kerman, Khorasan, Merv, Samarkand, Balkh, Kabul and Kashgar test inside. Tehran, western Iran, Quetta, Lahore, Almaty and Khotan test outside.

The target is absent at 2000 BCE, when its later footprint is divided among several atlas labels. Its tested membership stays stable at 1000 and 700 BCE although the coordinate count and hash change. At 500 BCE most sampled points become “Achaemenid Empire,” but Kashgar is blank. These are editorial seams, not instant ethnic conversions.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this exact umbrella and interval. Original script: unavailable. Transliteration: unavailable. Translation: unavailable. Proto-Iranian is reconstructed, the Avesta was orally transmitted and cannot be pinned to every mapped community, and Darius's first dateable Old Persian text at Bisotun belongs to a named western Achaemenid institution around 521 to 519 BCE, outside the footprint and too specific to represent this umbrella.

Archaeology studies artifacts and contexts; genetics models biological ancestry; historical linguistics reconstructs relationships among languages; texts record particular literate institutions. None is a magic label-maker for the others. Hundreds of ancient genomes reveal movement and mixture, yet they cannot tell which language one skeleton spoke or what an atlas color meant.

sections.title: Cross deserts, river fans, foothills and the roof of Central Asia

items.text: The polygon crosses Iran's dry eastern plateau, the Karakum and Kyzylkum deserts, Afghan basins and mountain corridors. Water was patchy, so settlement often clustered near springs, piedmont streams or river fans. The Merv dossier shows shifting channels and abandoned zones, but a dry spell never automatically explains a migration or political collapse.

In the Murghab oasis, silt spread into a fan where canals could steer water toward fields and settlements. Bronze Age centers such as Gonur and Iron Age centers such as Yaz Depe occupied different parts of that changing landscape. “Oasis” did not mean one city: small farms, camps, canals and larger mudbrick centers formed a network.

Ulug Depe stood by the Kopet Dag foothills, where a gorge linked plains and mountains. Its deep layers run from the Neolithic through the middle Iron Age. Excavated architecture and pottery change within one mound, making the site a useful time machine, but one mound cannot stand in for all Turkmenistan or the entire polygon.

The Pamirs and neighboring high valleys offered summer grass, narrow farmable terraces and difficult winter routes. Plant remains, pollen and charcoal show agropastoral landscapes built gradually, with cultivation and grazing at different elevations. Researchers still have sparse samples, so a highland corridor should not be drawn as a single seasonal highway used identically by everyone.

The atlas reaches Kashgar but stops before Khotan in the point tests. Farther around the Tarim and Kunlun margins, dated houses, barley, wheat, herds and riding gear reveal locally varied agropastoral communities. Genomes from Tarim burials also show distinctive ancestry. Those neighbors are comparisons, not proof that Kashgar shared their identity or language.

sections.title: Herd animals without turning every household into a nomad

items.text: At Ojakly and another camp on the Murghab desert edge, charred wheat, barley and broomcorn millet occur between roughly 1700 and 1200 BCE. The sites belonged to mobile herders near farming villages. Their crops may have been grown, exchanged or carried in different cases. Direct seeds break the false rule that movement and farming cannot mix.

Sheep, goats and cattle transformed grass and crop stalks into meat, milk, hides, dung and transport power. At Central Eurasian sites outside the core polygon, animal DNA and tooth isotopes show millet foddering alongside herding. That scientific comparison demonstrates one possible mixed strategy; it does not prove that every herd in Bactria ate millet.

In the high Alay Valley, ZooMS identified mostly sheep with smaller amounts of cattle and goat, while a nearby grinding stone suggests plant processing. This direct, mountain-specific case warns against a single “pastoral package.” Herd composition, elevation, season and access to fields changed the work calendar from one valley to another.

Iron Age Ulug Depe preserved plant and animal remains from a settled foothill community, while the larger regional literature also documents mobile camps and oasis villages. Archaeobotany and zooarchaeology can identify foods and livestock, but they rarely reveal whether one household owned an animal, borrowed it, tended another family's flock or received meat at a feast.

Domestic horse lineages spread widely through Eurasia during the second millennium BCE, and horses could pull vehicles, carry riders or serve as status animals and food. A horse bone does not automatically prove mounted nomadism. Researchers need age, sex, pathology, bit wear, gear and context before deciding how a particular animal worked.

sections.title: Cook meals that cross the farmer and herder stereotype

items.text: Wheat and barley brought cool-season calories; broomcorn millet ripened in warm months; peas supplied another plant food. Direct highland crop finds prove that cultivation reached difficult elevations, while Ulug Depe's plant remains anchor farming at one foothill settlement. Crop lists still do not reveal portions, recipes or who ate more in a household.

Milk can be drunk fresh, fermented or turned into foods that keep longer, but dairy must be demonstrated rather than assumed. Proteins trapped in dental calculus give direct evidence in some eastern steppe burials. Isotopes from Caucasus pastoralists show varied diets with plants and possibly fish alongside animal products. Both are regional comparisons, not a menu for Bactria.

Animal bones can reveal butchery, herd age and species; charred seeds show plants that reached a fire; grinding stones suggest crushing grain. None preserves a complete stew. People could roast meat, boil grain in pots, bake dough on hot surfaces or combine dairy and plants, but each recipe needs local residues, use-wear or experimental support.

Mineralized dental plaque is an accidental time capsule. Microscopic starch, phytoliths, proteins and microbes can become trapped on teeth, while cavities and wear record other parts of diet and daily work. Fun fact: ancient “tartar” can outlast the meal by thousands of years, though contamination and identification rules still matter.

Broomcorn millet has a short growing season and tolerates dry conditions, useful qualities where families moved or rainfall was uncertain. Yet a fast crop is not a “nomad grain.” Murghab and mountain evidence shows millet beside wheat, barley and peas. Fields, traded bags and animal fodder can leave different clues that researchers must separate.

sections.title: Sleep in camps, mudbrick homes and growing oasis centers

items.text: Gonur Depe largely belongs before or at the opening edge of this card, ending around 1500 BCE. A satellite settlement had ovens, kilns, household zones and more than seventy human and animal graves, plus a rare painted wall fragment. It is direct evidence for a complex oasis neighborhood, not an ancestral capital for every later Iranian speaker.

Iron Age Merv included Yaz Depe and Takhirbaj Depe among clusters of smaller settlements. Handmade painted vessels, mudbrick platforms and fortified centers help archaeologists name “Yaz” traditions. The name describes recurring material patterns, not a passport. Scholars disagree over how much change reflects migration, local transformation or interaction.

At Ulug Depe, excavators distinguish Yaz I and Yaz II occupations through architecture, pottery and stratigraphy. A high mudbrick platform and later citadel required planning and labor. Those features suggest organized communities, yet a big building alone cannot prove a king, taxation, forced labor or the language spoken by its builders.

Elsewhere, mobile camps could contain hearths, light shelters, corrals and storage that leave much thinner traces than a mudbrick mound. Large framed or semi-subterranean houses also existed in northern oasis regions. Mobility and settlement formed a spectrum: some people moved animals while relatives stayed near fields, and schedules could change between generations.

Canals, wells and river branches made desert settlement possible, and household waste likely went into pits, middens or reused outdoor spaces. The reviewed exact-period site reports do not establish one standard toilet, sewer or latrine for this umbrella. Absence of a named toilet feature means “unknown,” not that people ignored cleanliness or water safety.

sections.title: Shape metal, clay, fiber and long-distance connections

items.text: Bronze makers needed copper, tin, fuel, molds and practiced control of heat. Chemical and lead-isotope studies link artifacts and ores only probabilistically, because metal can be mixed and recycled. Central Asian tin and copper sources supported several routes. A matching alloy is evidence for technological connection, not proof of one merchant people or empire.

Iron did not flip an overnight switch called the Iron Age. Eastern Central Asian communities kept excellent bronze traditions while iron knives, sickles and needles appeared unevenly, especially in the ninth to sixth centuries BCE. Early iron could even be softer than good bronze. The achievement was learning new ores, furnaces, forging and repair over time.

Cloth rarely survives, but woven impressions pressed into pottery preserve thread spacing and structure. Spindle whorls, needles and awls supply more clues to spinning, sewing and repair. Such work demanded practiced hands and hours of labor. Archaeology cannot assign all textile work to women unless graves, tools, bodies and context support that local conclusion.

Museum collections include carved seals, metal vessels, stone ornaments and objects made with lapis lazuli or turquoise from southeastern Iran and western Central Asia. Style and material reveal connections, but many early objects lack secure excavation records. The safest stories begin with excavated contexts and treat beautiful unprovenanced pieces as limited evidence.

At Tepeh Ferizi in northeastern Iran, survey found artifacts spread across an approximately eighteen-hectare settlement related to earlier BMAC traditions. Erosion and movement rounded some sherds, reminding us that an object on today's surface may have shifted. Trade routes and cultural contacts must be reconstructed from many secure findspots, not a single wandering potsherd.

sections.title: Grow up inside households, neighborhoods and wider networks

items.text: A mudbrick house gathers traces of cooking, storage, craft and repair, but it is not a family tree. Residents might include partners, children, elders, other kin, guests, workers or dependents. Central Asian settlements and burials show varied domestic arrangements. They cannot supply one marriage rule, clan system or household size for the atlas umbrella.

Ancient DNA from one Ulug Depe person clusters with sampled BMAC individuals, while broader Uzbekistan studies find continuity plus later mixture. One genome is one life, and a genetic cluster is not an ethnicity. DNA cannot identify a person's spoken language, occupation, legal status or feelings about neighbors. Sampling and preservation also leave enormous gaps.

Gonur's cemetery includes many infants and children, making young lives archaeologically visible. Age-at-death and stress markers can show risks, but grave goods do not automatically name a child's rank or parents. Jar burials and other treatments documented across Central Asia differed by place and time, warning against one shared funerary rule.

Children learned by watching, trying, being corrected and helping with age-appropriate work. A later pottery-learning study shows how fingerprints, uneven shapes and skill stages may reveal apprenticeship, a labeled comparison rather than direct proof here. Herding, spinning, planting and water management also required long practice. No exact-period schoolroom or textbook is known.

Seals, monumental buildings and unequal grave goods may signal administration or status, but interpretation stays local. Gonur's satellite homes and graves show different activities around a large center; later Ulug Depe construction suggests coordinated labor. Neither establishes one pastoral aristocracy, inherited caste, tax system or coercive state across thousands of kilometers.

sections.title: Meet pain, care, water and the awkward toilet question

items.text: A study of 920 people from later Gonur contexts recorded dental abscesses, childhood cribra orbitalia, joint disease, infections and mostly accidental injuries; male skull trauma was more frequent. Those patterns suggest diet, workload and stress in one community. They are not a health report for every oasis, camp, sex or century inside the polygon.

One Gonur skeleton had unusual tumor-like lesions. Careful specialists compare shape, distribution and microscopic structure before suggesting a diagnosis, and even then one body cannot establish prevalence. The valuable discovery is also a lesson in restraint: ancient disease names are hypotheses, not labels that can be copied onto every painful bone.

People certainly soothed pain, set some injuries, assisted childbirth and used plants, heat, rest or ritual, but no securely identified medical manual or shared healer's kit belongs to this umbrella. Survival after injury may suggest care without revealing the treatment. A plant in a deposit is food, fuel or medicine only when context supports the choice.

Carbon and nitrogen isotopes can compare broad food inputs; strontium and oxygen can investigate movement when local baselines are known. The open North Central Asia database combines thousands of measurements with dates and contexts. Numbers are not biographies by themselves: environment, breastfeeding, animal fodder, preservation and reservoir effects all complicate interpretation.

No reviewed site report establishes a standard 1500 to 500 BCE toilet, sewer or hand-washing system for the entire footprint. People likely chose outdoor spots, pits or refuse areas and kept drinking water apart where possible. Archaeologists can test sediments, parasites and mineralized plaque, but “not found” must remain uncertainty rather than a joke about dirty ancestors.

sections.title: Ask about belief, authority, conflict and play without inventing answers

items.text: Buildings at Gonur and Togolok were once called Zoroastrian fire temples, but most specialists now reject that confident identification. Hearths, ash, special vessels and unusual rooms can mark ritual without naming a religion. Zoroastrian traditions have deep histories, yet an architectural resemblance cannot turn every Bronze or Iron Age community into an organized congregation.

The Avesta preserves Old Iranian language and religious poetry, but its oldest compositions were transmitted orally and its dating and geography remain debated. Memorized verse shows that writing is not required for sophisticated thought. It also means this card cannot print an Avestan line as a securely local voice from every place and century in the polygon.

Burials with ornaments, pottery, animals or unusual body treatment can express memory, affection, identity, fear or status. The same object may carry several meanings. Comparative Central Asian burial research documents great variation, including child jars and secondary treatment. It cannot translate a grave into one shared doctrine about gods or the afterlife.

Walls, arrowheads, daggers and male skull trauma show that defense and violence were possible. A fortified center may protect grain and families, display authority or organize refuge; a point may hunt or fight. Calling these finds an army, conquest or warrior ethnicity requires settlement destruction, human trauma, weapon context and chronology together.

Children almost certainly played, adults told stories and gatherings included music or humor, but no rulebook, toy label or punch line survives for this umbrella. A safer light fact comes from architecture: families lived beside buildings made from millions of handfuls of earth. Mudbrick was local, repairable and excellent insulation, though rain made maintenance everybody's recurring chore.

sections.title: Celebrate real achievements and let the map ending stay a map ending

items.text: Mixing wheat, barley, millet, peas and herding was a flexible achievement, not an indecisive halfway stage. Different crops ripened in different seasons and landscapes, while animals converted pasture and by-products into food and fiber. Direct plant and livestock evidence shows mobile families could help move crops across Asia without belonging to one trade empire.

Metalworkers linked geology to craft. They selected ores, made charcoal, controlled furnace air, cast bronze and learned to forge iron. Researchers now use elemental and isotope chemistry to reconstruct those networks. The achievement includes repair and recycling, which kept tools useful but can blur an artifact's original ore source for modern detectives.

Genome studies reveal continuity, movement and mixture rather than a clean replacement of one population by “Iranian pastoralists.” Late Bronze and Iron Age individuals across Turan and northern South Asia carry ancestry in different proportions. That complexity is the discovery. Genes are inherited biologically; languages, foods and identities are learned and can cross genetic boundaries.

At 500 BCE the atlas removes the exact target. Most tested points from Yazd to Balkh and Samarkand become “Achaemenid Empire,” while Kashgar is blank and nearby South Asian points receive other labels. This does not mean one pastoral people fell on New Year's Day. It records a coarse imperial-era redraw with no invented predecessor or successor chain.

Communities, herding routes, farms, languages and craft traditions continued beyond the card. Later Bactrian, Sogdian, Saka and Persian evidence belongs to distinct places and periods, and even the language map remains incomplete. Continuity can include political conquest and cultural change without turning diverse earlier households into a single nation marching toward an empire.

ending.text: At 500 BCE the atlas replaces the broad umbrella with the Achaemenid Empire across most tested points, other labels in neighboring South Asia, and a blank at Kashgar. Local people, crops, herds, settlements, languages and skills continued through uneven political change. The target did not share one fall, so the researched override keeps fell null and invents no predecessor or successor links.
